hook: With the Seljuk Turks overrunning Anatolia, the Byzantine emperor asked the West for help, and Pope Urban II called on Christians to march and recover Jerusalem.

sides.who: Knights, foot soldiers and pilgrims from France, Lorraine, Flanders and Norman Italy, helped at first by the Byzantine Empire
The Seljuk Sultanate of Rum in Anatolia, the Danishmendids, and the rival Turkish emirs of Syria such as Kerbogha of Mosul
The Fatimid Caliphate of Egypt, which had taken Jerusalem from the Turks in 1098

resultLine: The crusaders stormed Jerusalem on 15 July 1099 and, on 12 August, routed the Fatimid army sent to retake it at Ascalon.

strategies.name: The Byzantine alliance
strategies.text: At Nicaea in 1097 a Byzantine naval attack backed the crusaders' assault, and the city surrendered to the emperor. The alliance gave the princes a safe crossing into Asia and a firm start.

strategies.name: Treachery at Antioch
strategies.text: Antioch's walls were too strong to storm. In June 1098 Bohemond struck a secret deal with Firouz, a commander inside, who let a small party over the wall to open a gate for the army.

strategies.name: Exploiting Muslim divisions
strategies.text: Seljuk emirs in Syria were at odds with each other and with Fatimid Egypt, so they never united against the crusaders. Relief armies came one at a time, and each was beaten.

impact: Four crusader states were founded: Jerusalem, Edessa, Antioch and, in 1109, Tripoli.
After the victory most crusaders went home, leaving only about 300 knights and 2,000 foot soldiers to hold Palestine.
Saladin retook Jerusalem in 1187, and the last crusader strongholds on the mainland fell with Acre in 1291.
